clue.text: Combat manoeuvres – keeping watch regularly in caves?

definitions.note: A catacomb is one underground burial gallery, so the plural 'caves' is a loose gloss by example, which is what the question mark owns up to.

indicators.note: A manoeuvre shifts something into a new position, and troops on manoeuvres finish nowhere near where they set off.
'keeping' here is retaining: the shuffled letters take two more in with them instead of leaving them out.
'regularly' means at fixed intervals — every second letter of the word beside it, not all five of them.

blocks.note: six letters lifted straight off the clue, ready to be rearranged
taken at every other letter: the second and the fourth

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a military exercise, so 'Combat' reads as part of the picture rather than as the raw material. It is the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: A catacomb is a man-made cave system cut for burials, so the definition names it by its shape rather than its purpose.

clue.text: Tight biceps after lifting

indicators.note: 'lifting' hauls the word up the page, and a down entry read upwards is a down entry read the other way round.

blocks.note: 'guns' is gym slang for a well-developed pair of biceps

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a weights session, where lifting is what you do rather than what you do to a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Snug means close-fitting, the sense a garment has when it grips, rather than the cosy-room sense that comes to mind first.

clue.text: Question weaker body? Try exercising. (One probably sits with a computer all day)

definitions.text: One probably sits with a computer all day

indicators.note: A body put through its exercises is worked into one shape after another, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: the standard short form, as in Q and A
thirteen letters that come back in a different arrangement

explanation.walkthrough: 'One' pushes you towards a person — a coder, a gamer — and the definition turns out to be the object on the desk instead.
explanation.definitionFit: What sits with a computer all day is not the user but the slab of keys they type on, named for its top row.

clue.text: This suggests he took bat for discipline

indicators.note: The clue points at its own solution: the first word of it names what has been done to the three words after it.

blocks.note: the opening word is the instruction as well as part of the phrase
the same nine letters, hurled into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: A self-referential trick: the phrase carries the very verb that scrambles the rest of it, while 'he took bat' keeps the cricket surface going.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw the book at someone is to punish them with every charge available, which is disciplining them as hard as the rules allow.

clue.text: Imagine taking group of drivers north on M1 to see Coral’s relative?

indicators.note: 'taking' is taking in: the word in front of it swallows what follows instead of standing beside it.

blocks.note: to see something happening is to imagine it
the AA is Britain's Automobile Association, the motoring club that comes out to broken-down cars
the compass point's usual single letter
the motorway gives up its letter and then its number, spelled out

explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means sitting on top of, so the motorway goes underneath. The surface is a drive up the M1 to the coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Anemones and corals are both anthozoans, flower-shaped polyps of one class, so the definition claims a genuine family tie.

clue.text: Keep everything in pathetic pocketbook

indicators.note: To keep something somewhere is to store it there, so this is the instruction to house one word inside another.
'in' is doing literal work: the letters it introduces land inside the next word rather than after it.

blocks.note: in British use a wet person is feeble and spineless
the plain three-letter word for the lot

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a sad little purse. 'Pathetic' is not describing anything: it is supplying a schoolyard insult to build on.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Pocketbook' is the American name for the folding case that holds notes and cards, so it names the same object under another flag.

clue.text: A better plan – finally – to stop game hunters

indicators.note: 'finally' asks for the end of each word it governs — the letter each one finishes on.
To stop a pipe or a gap is to plug it, so one set of letters is pushed into the middle of another.

blocks.note: the game played on a green, which is then prised open
the closing letter of each of the three words, in the order they come

explanation.walkthrough: 'game hunters' begs to be read as one phrase about safari. Only the last word is the definition; the game is the one played on grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Barn owls take live prey, quartering fields at dusk for voles and mice, so 'hunters' names them by trade rather than by scavenging.

clue.text: Tesla isn’t working with NYC borough

indicators.note: Dough that is being worked is being pushed out of its shape, and that is what the letters here undergo.

blocks.note: nine letters as printed, the apostrophe counting for nothing
'with' joins two things exactly as 'and' does, and those three letters go into the mix too

explanation.walkthrough: 'isn't working' looks like the signal — a stalled electric car — and it is not: 'isn't' is material, and the joining word after it is material as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Staten Island is the least populous of New York City's five boroughs, joined to Manhattan by the free ferry.

clue.text: Bears controlling hunger – they eat carrion

indicators.note: To control something is to have it in your grip, so one word is holding another inside it.

blocks.note: to bear a resemblance is to have one
a yen is a craving, a hunger for something

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' looks like the animals sharing the sentence with the answer. It is the verb, and the dash keeps the nature-note disguise going.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyenas scavenge what bigger predators leave, so the definition names them by diet, the whole clause standing in for a plural noun.

clue.text: Crew fitting angle brackets

indicators.note: To bracket something is to fence it in on both sides, which is what the words either end of it are doing.

blocks.note: the letters run straight across the join between the two words

explanation.walkthrough: 'angle brackets' is a real thing in typing and computing, so the phrase reads as one unit and hides the seam it is pointing at.
explanation.definitionFit: A crew of labourers under one foreman is a gang, so the definition takes the workplace sense rather than the street-mob one.

clue.text: Just dread spending days working in dark

indicators.note: Spending is parting with what you have, so the word beside it parts with the letters named next.
'in' puts the piece it introduces inside the following word instead of alongside it.

blocks.note: D is the short form of day, and the plural means dread gives up both of its D's
sable is the heraldic word for black
a machine that is working has been switched on

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a night shift nobody wants. 'Just' does the definition's work in the very first word, which is where a solver least expects it.
explanation.definitionFit: A reasonable decision is a fair and defensible one, so this is the 'just' of justice, not the 'just' that means merely.

clue.text: Rogue bully by boxing ring

indicators.note: To box something is to shut it in a box, so the letter that follows goes inside rather than after.

blocks.note: to cow someone is to bully them into submission
the little word taken at face value, then split open
a ring is drawn as a circle, which is the letter O

explanation.walkthrough: 'boxing ring' is one thing in the surface and two instructions in the parse — nothing here is about the fight game.
explanation.definitionFit: In British use a cowboy is a shoddy, dishonest tradesman, so 'rogue' takes that sense and not the cattle hand of the surface.

clue.text: Mother might express this clumsily – be smart and kind

indicators.note: Handle something clumsily and it comes down in the wrong order, which is what has happened to these letters.

blocks.note: seven letters that come back in a different order
your ilk is your kind, the sort of people you belong among

explanation.walkthrough: 'be smart and kind' sounds like advice a mother would hand out, which is the whole disguise: the two halves do quite different jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Express' is the nursing verb for drawing off what a feeding mother produces, so the definition names the answer by how it is obtained.

clue.text: Two nurses ignoring half of my request

indicators.note: The word that follows is only two letters long, so ignoring half of it throws away the first and keeps the second.

blocks.note: the first of the pair is EN, Britain's enrolled nurse, a standing crossword abbreviation
the second is the verb: to nurse a patient is to treat one
the M is the half that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Two nurses' asks for two different words for the same job, one an abbreviation and one a verb — a common way to hide a short charade.
explanation.definitionFit: An entreaty is a request made with feeling, a plea rather than a routine asking, so the definition is the plain noun sense.

clue.text: Become the best by baking bread or a little rock cake

indicators.note: What goes into the oven as dough comes out as something else entirely, so this is the signal that the letters are recast.
'a little' wants only a small piece of the word beside it — its opening letter and nothing more.

blocks.note: seven letters straight into the mix
only the opening letter is wanted from this one
four more letters for the mix

explanation.walkthrough: 'rock cake' is a real bun, which is what makes the split so hard to see: those two words belong to different parts of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To break a record is to better the best mark anyone has set, which is exactly what becoming the best amounts to.

clue.text: See 3
See 15
Refinement represented Cecil Day …

indicators.note: Read it as re-presented: the same material put in front of you again, in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: eight letters handed over whole, ready to be rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The trailing dots run on into 21, where 'Lewis' completes the poet Cecil Day-Lewis — a name you need not know to solve either clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Refinement here is fineness of feeling or handling, the abstract quality, not the something-nice-to-eat sense the word also carries.

clue.text: See 8
Watches musical’s opening night – that’s when these things shine!

definitions.text: night – that’s when these things shine!

indicators.note: 'opening' is about place, not letters: the musical goes at the front, ahead of the word for watches.

blocks.note: the Lloyd Webber show that ran for decades in the West End
eyes watch, so the organ and the verb share a word

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive does the assembling: the musical's watches. In the surface, 'opening night' is a first performance, and the parse splits that phrase in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Cats-eyes are the reflective studs down the middle of a British road, and their glass beads throw headlight beams straight back after dark.

clue.text: … Lewis’s character – conclusively yet obliquely

indicators.note: A conclusion is an ending, so this asks for the letter the next word finishes on.

blocks.note: the lion who rules Narnia in C S Lewis's books
the final letter of the little word beside the instruction

explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots hand 'Lewis' back to 18, where Cecil Day is waiting: the two surfaces share one poet's name between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Aslant means set at a slant, so 'obliquely' matches it as an adverb: crossing at an angle rather than square on.

clue.text: Live in Le Mans – and the VW?

indicators.note: Le Mans is a French town, so the words after it are to be taken in French rather than English.

blocks.note: to live is to be
the French for and
the masculine French article, the one standing in the town's own name

explanation.walkthrough: The instruction hides inside a place name, and the 24-hour race there keeps the whole surface pointing at cars.
explanation.definitionFit: The Volkswagen sold as the Beetle is one model among the marque's many, which is what the question mark admits.

clue.text: See 4
Cartoon dog bites old woman clutching cat food in tins?

definitions.note: 'Food in tins' describes a whole shelf while the answer is one singular item, and the question mark is where the setter owns that looseness.

indicators.note: A bite closes the jaws around something, so the dog's word shuts around what comes next.
To clutch is to hold tight in the fist, and whatever is clutched sits inside the hand rather than beside it.

blocks.note: Disney's dog, Mickey's pet, five letters that then get prised apart
the familiar word for mother
a tomcat is the male of the species

explanation.walkthrough: 'cat food in tins' is a supermarket shelf and reads as one phrase; only the last three words are the definition, and the cat belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Plum tomatoes are the oval Italian sort sold tinned rather than fresh, so the definition points at them by their supermarket form.

clue.text: Large hole in one tie

blocks.note: the clothing size, and the standard abbreviation for it
a hole in one at golf is an ace

explanation.walkthrough: 'Large hole' looks like one idea and 'in one tie' like another; the break really falls between the size and the golfer's shot.
explanation.definitionFit: To lace a boot is to tie it, so the definition takes the verb sense rather than the cord you do it with.

clue.text: Decide to swap hands and draw

indicators.note: Hands are left and right, L and R in the usual shorthand, and swapping tells you those two letters change places.

blocks.note: a judge who rules on a point has decided it

explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' offers several meanings at once and the surface points at the sketching one; the pull is the sense the clue wants.
explanation.definitionFit: A lure draws fish to a hook or customers to a shop, so 'draw' is the pulling sense, not the sketch or the tied match.

clue.text: Part of stag party in strip club getting wrecked in just seconds

indicators.note: 'seconds' names a position, not a stretch of time — the second letter of each word — and 'just' says take nothing else.

blocks.note: the second letter of each of these two words, in order
the same again, two words further along
and the second letters of the final two close it off

explanation.walkthrough: 'strip club getting wrecked' reads like an anagram waiting to happen, and 'stag party' looks like one phrase — but the definition stops at 'stag'.
explanation.definitionFit: An antler is the branched bony horn a stag grows and sheds each year, so the definition names it as one part of the animal.

clue.text: Drive a good line in test of acceleration

blocks.note: the street sign's abbreviation, as written on an envelope
the clue's own letter, taken as it stands
G is the standard short form, as in a report-card grade
a race is a line of descent, a breed or a stock

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' is not the verb the surface wants but the word on a street sign, shortened, and the clue is assembled one small piece at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: A drag race is a standing-start sprint down a straight quarter-mile, run to see which car gathers speed fastest.
